title: Biggest Product of Any Three
statement:
Given an integer array nums with at least three numbers, choose three of them at different positions and multiply them. Return the largest product you can get.

The numbers may be negative or zero.

examples.why: All positive: the three largest win, 7 × 5 × 3.
Two negatives multiply into a positive: −8 × −6 × 4 = 192 beats the three largest, 4 × 2 × 1 = 8.
Every product is negative, so you want the one closest to zero: −2 × −3 × −4. The two-negatives trick gives −40 here.

hints: If every number were positive, the three largest would win. What can negative numbers do to that?
Two negatives make a positive. The best product is either the three largest numbers, or the two smallest (most negative) numbers times the largest.
You do not need a full sort: one pass can track the three largest and the two smallest values.

explain.intuition:
After sorting, only the two ends of the array matter. A big product needs big absolute values, and those sit at the ends. The sign decides which combination wins: three positives at the top, or the two most negative numbers (whose product is a large positive) times the largest number.

Comparing just those two candidates covers every case, including all-negative input: there the three largest values are the ones closest to zero, which is the best possible negative product.
steps: Track max1 ≥ max2 ≥ max3 and min1 ≤ min2 in one pass.
For each number, shift it into the right slot of the top three and of the bottom two.
Return max(max1 × max2 × max3, min1 × min2 × max1).
pitfalls: Taking only the three largest numbers. Two large negatives can beat them, as in [-8, -6, 1, 2, 4].
Multiplying the two smallest with the third largest instead of the largest.
Using absolute values to choose the three. With all negatives, the largest absolute values give the most negative product.

solutions.title: Try every triple
solutions.idea: Three nested loops over distinct positions, keep the best product.

solutions.title: Sort and compare two candidates
solutions.idea: After sorting, the answer is the three largest or the two smallest times the largest.

solutions.title: One pass, five trackers
solutions.idea: Keep the three largest and two smallest values seen so far; no sort needed.
